nd the easel.
- You paint at the easel: paint a chunk, look at the canvas, paint the
  next. Its tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- What is painted stays painted. There is no undo: paint over what you
  don't want.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count. The
  clock isn't a budget or a target.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by reflecting,
  flipping, rotating or translating another mask's or stroke's coordinates.
  A shape that mirrors another is drawn as its own shape, not as
  `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or `m:at(W - x, y)`.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  Entries stay as written.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

** Each chunk is its own Lua chunk:
  `p = pile{...}` is there in later chunks, `local p = ...` is not.
- **Randomness is deterministic.** `math.random`, `rand` and `randn` are
  reseeded at the start of every chunk from the canvas's seed and the
  chunk's number, and passes pick their own seeds the same way (pass
  `seed=` to fix one). A replay paints the same thing, and a failed chunk
  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. Entries already there stay as they were written; writing a note
doesn't advance painting time.

    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

I'll move on to thinking about water and land next, but first let the sky finish since the paint's still workable for blending; finishing touches like glazes and highlights can wait until it dries more.

I'm planning to keep working the sky while it's wet: fixing the wedge cloud's fringe and inner modeling, adjusting the horizon cloud bank's shape, and building up the sun's glow with warmer, brighter tones near the horizon. For the large cloud, I'm considering adding a cool shadow mass beneath the lobes and lighter gray-cream lobes in the middle to match the left side — though I'm also weighing whether to just repaint that cloud fresh with a different approach.

I'm thinking about treating each cloud lobe as a proper volumetric form with distinct lit and shadow sides, possibly using ellipsoid-based forms with lit/shadow masking to get organic cumulus shapes. But I catch myself worrying this risks violating the principle of painting real shapes and marks rather than computing an image through masks — I need to be careful not to just encode a picture indirectly through lighting values instead of actually drawing.

I decide a more painterly approach is better: block in the overall shape in mid-grey-violet, then build up lobes with warm cream scumbling strokes following the lobe's curve while blending wet into the shadow tones for soft transitions.

Continuing that logic, I plan darker reflected shadows underneath and warm light at the bottom edges, with lost-and-found edges — soft where cloud meets sky, crisp where sunlit — finishing with thick white highlight strokes. Before refining the clouds further, I realize I need to establish the sun glow and horizon first since they set the overall lighting, so I'll paint the bright near-white glow area with radial falloff near the horizon.

Now I'm reconsidering the horizon cloud bank itself — it currently reads as a flat, stiff strip across the whole width, so I want to break it into a more natural, ragged strato-cumulus layer: thicker and darker on the right where it merges with the existing cloud wedge, and thinner with light glowing through gaps toward the sun on the left, adding smaller elongated cloud shapes of varying sizes for irregularity.

I should stop deliberating and start executing — painting a warm radial sun glow around the disc at (300, 452) using opaque body strokes with soft lost edges, then moving on to fix the horizon bank.

The glow is spilling past the horizon into the ground and reads as a puffy blob rather than something radiating outward with soft falloff — I want the cloud bank to partially cover it instead. I'm being too piecemeal fixing individual elements, so I should step back and plan the whole sky composition more deliberately.

Honestly the sky right now is pleasant but weak — real sunset skies have deeper chroma variation, with dark blue at top, cooler mid-tones, warm orange near the horizon, and dark cloud silhouettes for contrast. I'm thinking of shifting toward a stormier, more dramatic mood: darkening the upper sky and cloud deck while letting the low sun break through intensely at the horizon, throwing a golden path across the water — closer to a Turner or Ruisdael composition. Since the paint is still wet I can rework it directly, letting new opaque strokes mix into what's already there.

I'm mapping out target values for each zone — darker sky top and corners, a much brighter horizon glow, dark cloud masses with lit edges, silhouetted land, and water that reflects the light path while staying dark in the foreground. The current horizon glow is just a soft cream blob, so I want to refine it into an actual sun disc, partly veiled by a thin cloud strip, with a glow radiating outward.

The glow should warm toward orange (chrome yellow plus vermilion) further from center, with the surrounding sky shifting toward greenish-blue. Let me zoom into that area to check how the paint texture reads at full resolution.

The glow layer looks like a soft, blended underlayer with a pale cream edge, good enough to build the land and water over. Now I want to move to the composition basics—laying in the ground and water masses first, since they'll anchor the rest of the scene, starting with the tan primed ground in the lower portion of the image.

Checking the horizon placement, the sky I've painted down to about y=500 should read as roughly 68% down the canvas, consistent with a two-thirds sky composition, even though the original pencil line was drawn slightly higher and is now sealed beneath the paint. Next I'll layer in the water with a medium-dark blue-grey-green base topped with sky reflections and ripples, then add the distant shoreline with cooler, faded tones for depth, including a headland with trees and a windmill on the right.

For the foreground I'm planning dark umber-green reeds along the left bank, a wooden post, and a small fishing boat crossing the glare path — likely a Dutch botter-style vessel with a russet lug sail, dark hull, and a reflection below, placed at a waterline roughly 40 units under the horizon to read as mid-distance. Now I'm working out the scale relationships between the boat's mast height and hull length against the horizon line before turning to the shimmering light path spreading across the water from the sun's position.

I'm thinking through how the sky mirrors onto the water — the cloud bank and the large cloud mass reflecting as darker, softened horizontal strips broken by ripple streaks, with the brightest warm glow sitting just under the sun's position and fading into blue-grey toward the edges. I'll build this reflection in layers, starting with a broad flat horizontal underlayer matching the sky's colors before adding the streaked ripple texture on top.

Now I'm working out the water's color scheme from top to bottom: a pale warm glow near the horizon using lead white, yellow ochre, and chrome, transitioning into a blue-grey-green mid-tone beneath the widening light path, then deepening into a dark blue-grey (smalt, umber, prussian blue, white) toward the foreground, with an even darker greenish-brown near the bottom corners.

I'm mapping out the land forms: a dark blue-green-violet headland with a tree clump and windmill on the right side of the horizon (hazier at its left tip), and a pale violet-grey spit of land low on the left. Since the sky paint is still wet, I'm considering whether to let it set first before adding the land silhouette on top, to avoid muddying the horizon edge while keeping it crisp.

Waiting a day or two for the sky to dry costs nothing since time only passes when I choose, but I want to finish key wet-blending work on the sky (like softening cloud edges) first, then let it dry before painting crisp land and water shapes, saving any final sky glazes for after.

My priorities for the still-wet sky: deepen the top blue with a corner vignette, refine the wedge cloud's soft fringe and lit lobes, reshape the horizon bank and its glow, add rhythm with a small cloud and maybe extra cirrus wisps, and place the sun. I'm starting with a richer glaze for the upper sky, mixing a deep blue pile from smalt, Prussian blue, lead white, and raw umber with a transparent medium to darken and enrich that top zone before blending it in.

The glaze blend has smeared the small cloud along with darkening the sky, since everything is still wet and blending together. I need to take stock: blend softens wet paint effectively, but I'm losing definition on smaller shapes when the whole canvas is open at once.

Rather than fuss more with the sky in isolation, I should block in the major masses—land and water—so I can judge overall balance, then come back to refine the sky once it's set enough to layer on top without disturbing it. Looking at what the sky still needs: the sun glow is a bit too big and flat and could use more brightness at its center, and the big cloud on the right needs more definition as a dark mass.

I want to give that cloud more sculptural form, with lit tops facing the sun and a darker interior, using the cumulus shape (cumA) I defined earlier with its silhouette, lit, and shadow layers. I recall painting cumA's silhouette and shadow in earlier chunks but then wiping it with sky paint—I'm not sure how that attempt actually looked since I never properly viewed the result, and I'm noticing some of my earlier "looks" didn't display images at all, just filenames.

Maybe it's about parallel tool calls: when paint and look are invoked together, the look result comes back as "an earlier look" without an image, but when called standalone the image actually displays. That would explain why look-0011 onward showed images while the first batch didn't.

I think I should switch to making paint and look calls sequentially rather than in parallel, since parallel execution might mean look captures the state before paint finishes rather than after.

Now I want to re-examine the entire canvas to check whether my earlier blind painting caused any issues before deciding on next steps.

-- Repaint the horizon zone as one continuous coat: overlapping x-slices with triangular weights, so no seams.
function mixp(a, b, t, med)
  -- a, b: lists of {tube, parts}; linear interpolation of the parts by t
  local parts, names = {}, {}
  for _, e in ipairs(a) do parts[e[1]] = (parts[e[1]] or 0) + e[2] * (1 - t); names[#names+1] = e[1] end
  for _, e in ipairs(b) do
    if parts[e[1]] == nil then names[#names+1] = e[1] end
    parts[e[1]] = (parts[e[1]] or 0) + e[2] * t
  end
  local out = {}
  for _, n in ipairs(names) do
    if parts[n] > 0.01 then out[#out+1] = {n, parts[n]} end
  end
  out.medium = med or 0.08
  return pile(out)
end
function slices(y0, y1, A, B, wd, sd, ramp, n, tspan)
  n = n or 8
  for i = 0, n do
    local cx = 1000 * i / n
    local t = clamp(cx / (tspan or 1000), 0, 1)
    local hw = (1000 / n) * 1.15
    hb(rect(cx - hw, y0, 2 * hw, y1 - y0), mixp(A, B, t), wd, sd + i, 3.0, {60,150}, {load_at=function(x, y)
        local wx = clamp(1 - math.abs(x - cx) / hw, 0.03, 1)
        local wy = clamp((y - y0) / ramp, 0.05, 1) * clamp((y1 - y) / ramp, 0.05, 1)
        return wx * wy end})
  end
end

function slices2(y0, y1, A, B, wd, sd, ramp_top, ramp_bot, x0, x1, n, cov, span, med)
  for i = 0, n do
    local cx = x0 + (x1 - x0) * i / n
    local t = clamp(cx / (span or 800), 0, 1)
    local hw = ((x1 - x0) / n) * 1.2
    local rx0 = math.max(cx - hw, x0 - 30)
    hb(rect(rx0, y0, cx + hw - rx0, y1 - y0), mixp(A, B, t, med or 0.02), wd, sd + i, cov or 4.0, {60,150}, {load_at=function(x, y)
        local wx = clamp(1 - math.abs(x - cx) / hw, 0.02, 1)
        if i == 0 then wx = wx * clamp((x - x0 + 20) / 60, 0.0, 1) end
        local wy = clamp((y - y0) / ramp_top, 0.02, 1) * clamp((y1 - y) / ramp_bot, 0.05, 1)
        return wx * wy end})
  end
end

  for i = 0, n do

function cband(lo, hi, s)
  return mask(function(x, y)
    if x < 560 or y > 400 or y < 30 then return 0 end
    if cumsil:at(x, y) < 0.5 then return 0 end
    local v = cm:value(x, y)
    local a = smoothstep(lo - s, lo + s, v)
    local b = 1 - smoothstep(hi - s, hi + s, v)
    return a * b
  end)
end

events.name: look
events.text: size 1200

Taking stock of where things stand: the sky gradient looks good, but the cumulus cloud on the right has some flat, blocky facets that need softening, especially at its base. The pale sun glow near the left horizon seems worth revisiting too.

The sun feels too diffuse and needs a brighter, hotter focal point with more contrast, maybe with dark strata crossing the glow, though my earlier attempts at that looked more like a lumpy cotton shape. There's also a hard, abrupt edge where the right shore's silhouette begins, and the water still needs real work — reflections of the hill, a path of light, and cleanup of some odd leftover streaks near the bottom.

I'm considering swapping any harsh cloud bars for a softer, wispy warm-lit stratus layer done with fine horizontal strokes to reinforce the sunset mood, and planning the water's glitter path down from the sun along with reflections of the hill, grove, and clouds, plus a darker cool foreground for depth. I also want to add a small dark sailboat silhouette near the light path as a focal point, and maybe a tiny windmill on the right knoll for scale and story, though rendering the sails finely will take care.

Stepping back and squinting at the composition, I realize the value range feels too compressed overall -- the sky, clouds, horizon, and water are all sitting in a similar light-to-mid range -- so my priority should be darkening the foreground water with subtle ripples and reflected color to create real depth, then layering in the light path, the boat, and the hill reflection on top of that stronger structure.

The right half of the water has visible blur streaks and a dotted lattice pattern from thin paint, so I should repaint it with opaque coverage for better quality since it's dry now. I'm also pausing to think about the overall plan for the rest of the painting given how many chunks I've already used.

For the water, I'm planning a layered horizontal approach: a warm cream horizon-glow band near the top, cooling to blue-grey below, with a broken vertical zone of bright dashes marking the sun's reflected light path. I'll add the cumulus cloud's reflection as lighter warm-grey masses with mauve shadow, a dark broken-stroke reflection of the shore/grove, and fine horizontal ripple dashes growing denser toward the bottom.

For the sun, I want a smaller, hotter core right at the horizon with thin warm cloud strata and glitter across the water. For the boat, I'm placing a small silhouetted sailing barge with a red-brown sail at mid-distance, its mast and sail overlapping the horizon glow for contrast, scaled against the windmill on the knoll. For the foreground, I'm considering a dark spit of land, reeds, or a moored rowboat with a fisherman to anchor the composition.

I'm also thinking of adding tall reeds at the bottom-left for depth and a pair of dark wooden mooring piles at bottom-right with reflections and splash rings, giving human scale and vertical contrast against the horizontal water. The overall story I'm building is a calm evening estuary with a sailboat crossing toward the sun and mooring posts framing the scene.

For the cumulus cloud, I want to soften its flat, blocky planes with warm rim lighting facing the sun and cooler shadowed areas, maybe adding a glazing pass. I might also add tiny bird silhouettes near the sun for scale, but that's optional -- first I'll zoom into the cloud to see what needs fixing.

The clouds have good texture, but I'm noticing hard-edged cutoffs where the lit-face mask boundaries created cookie-cutter facets, plus faint ghost arcs left over from the older cloud shape in the sky. I need to smooth these transitions out.

Since the paint has dried, I'll soften those hard boundaries with a glaze or scumble in the neighboring color, or repaint sections wet-into-wet to properly blend them. Given the cumulus occupies a major focal quarter of the composition, it's worth redoing the middle sections with fresh opaque paint — thinking about real sunset cumulus lighting, with warm creamy lit tops, grey-lilac shadowed undersides, and soft billowy edges that turn crisp only where puffs overlap, built up through wet-in-wet dabbing strokes.

I'm considering hand-drawing around fourteen individual puffs as circles, each with a lit crescent cap and shadow crescent, blended locally and layered front-to-back — a more painterly approach than computed shading. Alternatively, I could rebuild the cloud by laying a fresh mid-value warm grey-lilac base coat over the whole silhouette first, covering the old dried paint while preserving the outer edge shape.

For clipping edges cleanly against the sky, I'll shrink the silhouette mask slightly so new paint stays contained and the existing edge quality is preserved. Then I'll add the puffs using short scumbled strokes, lighting the side facing the low sun on the left and shading the opposite side, though I need to think through exactly how the low horizon light angles across the cloud's form.

Since the sun sits right at the horizon and the viewer faces toward it, this cloud is actually backlit — light travels from behind, so the far side facing the sun gets bright silvery rims while the near side facing us falls into shadow. That means the brightest highlights should trace the left edges and top contours where the sun grazes through, while the body facing the viewer stays darker and more muted, with the surrounding sky glowing brightest near the horizon itself.

The base of the cloud reads well with its flat, dark lilac edge, so the main issue is the hard-edged facets rather than the overall shape or lighting. I'm thinking about repainting soft gradations over those facets and identifying the specific problem spots, like the center-left arc, to smooth them out and reduce the repetitive puffy look.

I could also try stippling with feathering to blend the boundary softly, or laying a ribbon of mixed intermediate color along each hard edge and blending it while still wet. But honestly, it might be better to scrap the local fixes and repaint the whole cloud form fresh with a new wet base, opaque enough to rebuild it with softer, larger shapes and backlit rims — more work, but it lets me improve the design rather than just patch it.

Now I want to set priorities for the rest of the painting: the water needs a full repaint since it's weak, the sun and left horizon need reworking, the cumulus needs rebuilding, and the boat, posts, and windmill need detail work — all before I get to final glazes, birds, glitter, and small signature touches. I'm also thinking about the overall value structure — this is a bright, high-key picture with the hill and grove as the dark anchor, and the upper-left sky reading blue.

Since water dominates roughly a third of the canvas, I'm working out its mirror-like reflection logic: each point on the water should echo the sky color at the mirrored elevation above it, so the water near the horizon glows warm while the lower water reflects a paler, bluer sky higher up.

But because Fresnel reflectance drops at steeper viewing angles, the lower water should blend that pale reflected sky with the water's own darker teal-grey body color, landing on a mid-dark blue-grey. I'm also mapping where the cumulus clouds would reflect down into the lower portion of the water based on their vertical position in the sky.

I'll hand-paint the reflected cloud masses as their own rough horizontal strokes rather than mirroring the sky shapes directly, since ripples break reflections into broken horizontal dashes. I'm also placing a bright sun-glitter column of white-yellow horizontal dashes running down the water near the horizon glow area.

Now I'm working out the darker reflected bands — shore, grove, boat, posts — and considering a subtle cooler, darker vignette toward the bottom corners to suggest water depth and the dark upper sky reflected far out.

I'm also weighing whether to add mooring posts or reeds as a foreground anchor, but I want to avoid overloading the right side, which already carries the clouds and hill — so a dark foreground element on the lower left might better balance the composition against the sunlit boat and open water.

I'll add a tuft of reeds at the bottom-left corner too. For the boat, I'm placing it mid-ground just right of the light path so its silhouette—dark reddish-brown sail, dark hull, with reflection below—overlaps the glitter for strong contrast, plus a small windmill on the far hill. For the sun itself, since the current glow is diffuse, I want to punch in a brighter, hotter white-yellow core near x=300 to give the composition a clear focal point.

Now I'm working out the sun disc: a small bright core ellipse, half-cut by the horizon, painted opaque with lead white and a touch of chrome yellow, surrounded by larger warm yellow-to-apricot halos. The wet blending kept making the halos look blotchy since it only affected the new layer, so the glow reads too weak right now. I'm thinking I need to darken the surrounding horizon sky slightly so the pure white sun disc pops with more contrast.

Glaze layers accumulate with medium-high transparency but earlier attempts produced a flat, plateau-like blob rather than a true radial glow. The horizon gradient worked well using narrow horizontal slices blended together, so maybe the sun glow needs a similar wet-into-wet approach painting concentric bands all at once rather than building up in passes.

Turner's sunsets work through contrast — a brilliant sun against dark silhouettes like boats and cloud bands, with a reflection column below. So darkening the distant shoreline sliver near the horizon and adding a thin dark cloud strata could sharpen the sun's brilliance instead of relying on a heavy gradient.

My first attempt at a cloud strip came out looking like a sausage because the shape was too uniform and the color too flat. A better approach uses thin, streaky strata with ragged, dry-brushed edges, several short strips at varying heights that taper off, mostly horizontal with low contrast except where they meet the sun's glow — using mauve-grey for the body and warm orange underlighting to make each stroke feel hand-dragged rather than filled in.

Given how much work is left and no way to undo mistakes, I need to plan my sequence carefully: sky and sun first (since water reflects them), then rebuild the cumulus clouds, add the distant shore and windmill, paint the water, then the boat, posts, and birds, finishing with final touches. Since the sky is dry now, I'll paint the sun's glow as a fresh wet gradient to keep it smooth.

For blending technique, I'm thinking about how a clean badger brush passing over wet paint fuses colors by lifting and moving them, which is what smoothed the sky bands earlier. For the sun's halo, I layered three ellipses with soft edges and blended them, but the result came out too flat because the colors were too close to the cream background -- I need to push the contrast to make the glow actually visible.

I need stronger saturation in the halo, like a chrome yellow core fading to white, paired with a cooler, darker sky nearby to make the glow pop against it. I'm reconsidering the whole sunset composition: apricot and gold near the horizon, transitioning up through cream-yellow to pale blue, with a lilac-peach fade horizontally away from the sun -- the effect currently exists but is too subtle, so I want to repaint the horizon band with more scale and contrast.

I'll define color bands by y-position -- warm gold near the horizon strongest at the sun's x-position fading to apricot on the sides, yellow-cream above that, and a white-hot core for the sun itself -- blending everything horizontally using a distance-based color mixing function centered on the sun.

For the sun itself, I'm picturing it as a small half-disc sitting right on the horizon line (center at x=300, y=497, radius ~13), only the upper half visible, with radiating glare and a bright reflection column beneath it -- this should read as more dramatic and clear than just a glow.

Above that, I want a few wispy horizontal cloud strata at different heights across the glare zone, mauve-grey with warm undersides, painted with dry brush strokes so contrast increases closer to the sun. Then I still need to address the cumulus shape and add some faint arc-like cloud forms in the upper left sky.

Locating those ghost arcs more precisely - they're the remnants of the old cumulus crown peeking out from behind the new one, darker blue than the surrounding sky. I'll need to match the exact sky gradient color at that height to paint over them cleanly, wet in wet.

The earlier translucent coat (smalt/cobalt with low medium) let the darker underlying paint show through, so this time I need to mix in lead white for full opacity and truly hide those arcs.

I need to work step by step since I can't preview results before painting. First, I'll target the sky ghost arcs near the cumulus with an opaque mixture, estimating the local color as a mid-blue around #6688b8 near the top and paler toward the horizon, though I'm second-guessing whether these subtle darker curves even need full correction since they might just read as a faint ghost cloud form in the final composition.

Since I'll be reworking the sky around the cumulus anyway during its rebuild, I'll fix both together — laying fresh opaque puffs over the dried old paint, keeping the existing silhouette as a rough guide but wanting sharper cauliflower-style lobes with crisp inner creases rather than smooth ellipsoid edges.

Better yet, I should keep the silhouette and just re-model the interior with soft-edged strokes over a wet base coat to avoid the hard facet edges left by masked paint bands. My plan: lay a warm mid-tone base across the interior first, then add soft lilac shadow crescents beneath each puff, followed by light accents on top.

I realize now why those facet edges appeared -- the form-based band masks create discontinuities where ellipsoids intersect, producing physically-plausible but too-hard creases at the union boundaries. To fix this I need to soften those crease lines by reworking them while the paint is still wet.

Alternatively, I could try a simpler approach: lay down one mid-lit base color across the whole cloud, then build puffs using a scumble/stipple technique with a filbert brush for natural cauliflower texture. I'm leaning toward the puff-by-puff method with hand-drawn outlines despite the extra passes required, since I can handle it with loops defining each puff's position, radius, and squash, generating an ellipse mask per puff.

I'm working out how to give each puff irregular, organic lobes using parametric points generated from cos/sin rather than copying another shape's coordinates, then figuring out lighting by offsetting a lit-cap mask toward the lower-right for a highlight effect.

With one parameter, offset is likely grow/shrink rather than translation, so instead of trying to translate a mask I should just build the crescent as a fresh shape—defining a second ellipse at its own offset position and combining it with the first via intersection or difference, which is the standard way to construct a crescent without moving another mask's coordinates.

I want to prioritize work now: focus first on water, sun, and the boat/posts since those give the biggest visual payoff, then circle back to the cumulus clouds if time allows. I'm also checking the horizon geometry — the waterline starts around y=497, and on the left there's a small mauve conical hill shape near x=410 that I want to make sure reads correctly against the shore.

That tiny pointed shape I placed near the far shore could work nicely as a distant church spire rather than a plain hill, adding a nice detail against the shoreline. Now I'm planning the sun's glow as a single wet painting pass over a broad sky region, layering opaque color in a gradient that radiates outward from the sun's position, wider horizontally than vertically to get that soft glow effect.

I'm working out the exact mix of lead white, chrome yellow, vermilion, and yellow ochre at each distance from the sun to move smoothly from white-hot at the center through golden yellow and apricot tones toward the edges of the glow.

I'm thinking through painting the halo as a series of nested ellipses from largest to smallest, each with soft "lost" edges and slight color steps, planning to blend them together afterward to avoid visible banding or a flat plateau look within each ring.

An alternative approach would use `load_at` as a smooth function of radial distance, letting deposit thickness vary continuously for a true airbrush-style glaze rather than discrete rings—though I recall this approach produced blotchy, dark drag artifacts in earlier attempts with chrome yellow glazes.

I'm not entirely sure whether that dark smear came from the glow blend dragging wet paint or from a partially dried hill layer underneath. Either way, the sky near the sun currently reads pale, so I should check the actual colors there before deciding how much more to layer in.

Technique lessons: (1) blend with a soft mask whose interior partly overlaps *dry* paint is fine, but blending with a rect mask at clip=false drags paint out over its edges; (2) `hb` slices with load_at ramps are a reliable way to build gradients; (3) always let things dry (wait 5+ days) before overpainting so lower layers don't come up.

For the cloud design, I'm planning a large cumulus on the right side, rising from the horizon with its top cropped near the upper corner and its base separated from the shore by a glowing gap, balancing the sun on the left. I want softer edges with strong rim lighting and a few smaller satellite cloudlets drifting toward the sun's glow to tie the composition together.

I'm now weighing a Turner-style approach: a long, low dark cloud bank spanning the horizon around y 400–470, broken by cracks of sunlight with the disc partially hidden behind it, giving the big cumulus something to rise above and grounding the whole sky. I'll proceed piece by piece, sketching each cloud as a hand-drawn soft outline with enough points to feel billowy.

Now I'm plotting the exact contour of the large cumulus mass, tracing its base, right edge, and lobed top in canvas coordinates to build a layered billow shape.

With the silhouette established, I'm thinking through how to add scalloped bulges at lobe centers for texture, then working out lighting logic — since the sun sits low on the horizon, light hits the cloud nearly horizontally from the left, making the lower-left faces warmly lit while the tops stay comparatively cooler.

I'm settling on a tonal scheme: warm cream/white crescents on the sunlit left faces, pinkish-grey mid-body, cool violet-grey shadow on the right/underside, darker mauve at the base, and peach reflected light along the bottom rim. Then I plan the wet-in-wet paint sequence, starting with a mid-tone body mass as the base layer.

Since the cloud silhouette meets the dry sky in a hard boundary, clipping to the mask gives crisp outlines, but I want some edges softer. There's an edge-blending option that distributes found/soft/lost shares along the contour, letting strokes fade past the boundary into the weave rather than cutting sharply — perfect for the parts of the cloud that dissolve into the sky.

For the lit crescents, I'm defining each lobe as a closed outline with hand-placed points, maybe 8 major lobes, each split into a lit upper-left arc and a shadowed lower-right arc. That's roughly 100 points if done manually, so I'm weighing whether to instead construct the lobes procedurally using circle and offset-ellipse masks.

I'm considering defining a crescent as one ellipse minus a slightly offset, smaller ellipse, with the offset direction hand-chosen per lobe based on where the light source sits. That raises a question about whether specifying two independent ellipses with different centers really counts as "translating" one shape's coordinates, since the rule against reflecting or translating masks might technically apply here.

I'm leaning toward varying each ellipse's radii and center so they're genuinely distinct shapes rather than exact copies, since the restriction seems aimed at mirrored duplicates of symmetrical parts. My earlier approach of computing tone bands directly from ellipsoid lighting looked too mechanical and noisy, so now I'm thinking about adding roughening to break up the regularity, or possibly painting the lit crescents as brush strokes instead of hard-edged masks.

Working out the stroke geometry along each lobe's upper-left arc...

Actually maybe I should lean less cauliflower, more stratocumulus bank — but the cumulus tower's solid scale contrast against flat sky/sea works well. The real issue is the "sticker" look from uniform crisp edges and stark light-against-dark value; real sunset cumulus has soft vaporous shadow edges, crisp only at the brightest rims, with the sky glowing lighter near those lit edges from scattering. I'll vary edges — crisp on the lit left side, lost/soft on the top-right and base — and make sure the shadow tone reads darker than the surrounding sky.

I'm setting the sky at that height to a medium light blue, the cloud shadows to a mauve-grey, and the lit side to a warm cream, giving the cloud more value range than the sky so it reads as solid volume. The sun disk itself won't be visible, just its glow, maybe with a subtle bright core. I'm also considering placing a long thin dark stratus bar low across the glow near the horizon with a reflection in the water, but I'll hold off on that until the cumulus is finished. First I need to let the sky patch dry, then paint the shore's silhouette dry-on-dry since it sits in front of the sky and cloud base.

I'll paint the shore before the cloud since the order doesn't matter but the shore is more straightforward -- a low spit of land starting around x=690 with a windmill, a grove of trees further right, and reed banks along an irregular top line, with the windmill rendered as a truncated cone with a cap and four sails.

My previous attempt at the silhouette with the outline and dark fill looked decent, and the windmill worked reasonably well though the tower felt a touch undersized. This time I want to tighten the proportions -- sail span around 36 units, tower closer to 30 tall, sitting against a horizon at 497 -- and render the whole thing in a very dark cool brown-black with warm rim light catching the left-facing edges.

I'm settling on tower base near y≈490, top around y≈456, with sails centered at the same height and a radius near 26 -- big enough to stay readable against the peach horizon without overpowering the distant, small-scale feel I want for the shoreline. The dark silhouette reads well against that warm background, so now I'm placing a cluster of dark rounded tree crowns along the shore to the right of the mill.

For the trees, I'm scrapping the earlier speckled, lit-up look and going with pure dark silhouettes instead, adding just a thin warm rim-light stroke on the left edge of each crown and a scalloped top rather than visible green speckle or twig detail, since fine texture wouldn't read at this distance. I'm also thinking about adding light stippling along the top edges to soften the silhouette into a feathery, foliage-like outline.

Now I'm plotting out the coastline coordinates point by point, sketching the land's curved profile from the horizon tip past the mill base and grove, then placing individual tree crowns as ellipses sitting along that land line with their own center points and radii.

Plotting tree coordinates...

I'm placing the mill near the grove's left edge at ground level, then thinking about small compositional touches like reflections in the water and a warm apricot rim light catching the left-facing sides of the tree crowns since the sun sits low and to the left.

I need the horizon line where water meets shore to read crisply, so I'll let the sky patch dry for about a week before painting the shore.

This looks more like a rocky hill than a tree grove since the outline forms a smooth peak, but the bottom has a scalloped fringe hanging below the horizon line where the shore meets the water. I'll need to clean up that bottom edge later by repainting the water's top line.

For the trees to actually read as trees, I need separate rounded crowns of varying heights with gaps of sky between them rather than one smooth ridge—each crown maybe 14-20 wide, with the tallest peak sitting well above the horizon. I'll redraw the skyline with bumps every few units to create that scalloped foliage silhouette.

I'm sketching a specific arrangement to make it feel distinctly Dutch: three thin poplars in a row (narrow vertical shapes about 8 wide and tall), then a couple of rounder trees beside them, low bushes trailing off along the bank, and I'm considering adding a small farmhouse with a red-tiled roof for extra character.

Since the hillside shape is now solid, I'll need to repaint over parts of it with sky color to reshape the silhouette, covering the old peak with the peach and cream gradient used elsewhere in the sky.

I could paint peach coverage over the hill's dark surface to lower its silhouette, then let it dry before adding the new shoreline on top. Or, simpler, I could just paint new tree crowns directly over the existing dark mound without covering it first — the old shape would just read as the lower hedges/mass beneath new treetops.

I need the right side to match the apricot tone near the horizon and the left to stay cream-yellow, so I'll paint the small region in four vertical slices with interpolated tints and let them blend horizontally in the wet paint.

events.text:
I'm puzzling over why the dark smudged up into the peach layer — wondering if it's because the black paint underneath hadn't fully dried yet since I'd only painted the shore about forty minutes earlier, and whether bone black's slow drying time is the culprit.

Confirming: bone black dries slowly (0.4 relative rate), so the shore paint was still open when I dragged my cover strokes over it, smearing the dark into a dirty cloud over the peach. The lesson is clear — bone black stays wet for days, so I should have waited before painting over it. Since the whole area is wet now and not salvageable as-is, I'll give it roughly ten days to fully dry before repainting the sky above the mound with a fresh cover coat, then adding the trees.

The sky gradient looks clean now but the painting feels too empty with just sky and water. I need to fix that stray pink strip at the horizon and rebuild the shore silhouette, since the hill and windmill got painted over and need to come back.

For clouds I should try painting a new wet layer directly onto the dry sky, using soft-edged brushwork and keeping blends clipped inside slightly-oversized masks so the fusion stays contained rather than dragging paint unpredictably — the earlier failure came from letting the blend clip go outside the mask, creating harsh rims.

Actually, maybe the towering cumulus approach is fundamentally too hard given the cut-out silhouette and cauliflower interior I got before. A simpler, more atmospheric solution might work better: long, low horizontal stratocumulus bars lit from below by the sun, rather than fighting with a complex layered cloud form.

Let me step back and assess what's actually on the canvas now — a tall gradient sky, warm and luminous on the left, cool blue above, water below with pale glow darkening at the bottom. Building on that, I'm considering adding a few thin, wispy cloud strata across the mid-sky with sunlit edges, plus a stronger cloud mass at the upper right.

I'm also picturing a distant shoreline with a windmill silhouette at the right, a boat crossing the light path, glittering reflections on the water, and dark reed or post silhouettes in the foreground at left/bottom. Rather than building clouds from ellipsoid forms, I should paint them directly with painterly, soft-edged brushstrokes and low-coverage glazes for softness, moving away from my overly smooth, blended technique toward more visible brushwork character throughout.

Now I need to fix the water color near the horizon — the current pink strip is too vermilion-heavy compared to the paler, greyer water on the left side and the soft pink-grey reflection expected on the right where the sky's warmth shows through.

Physically, the horizon reflection should be a bright pink-cream band that fades to blue-grey water below, since water reflects near-horizon sky brightly due to Fresnel effects. My hard-edged rectangle looks wrong against that though, and since the paint's already dry I can't blend it smooth — I'll need to add more strokes on top that fade downward to soften that lower edge.

Now I'm planning the cloud composition: a dark grey-mauve mass top-right with warm sunlit edges, a stratus bank along the horizon near the sun broken into perspective-diminishing bars, and light wispy cirrus strokes in the upper sky glowing peach from below.

I also want to push the value contrast harder — the picture's too mid-toned overall, so I'll deepen the lower third with heavy dark foreground shapes (reeds, bank silhouette) at the corners to frame the glow. For composition, I'm placing the sun at 30% from left with the shore and windmill on the right and cumulus top-right, and considering adding a small dark sailboat near the edge of the light path for a classic silhouette effect.

For the foreground I'll keep it simple rather than overloading it — a dark reed bed silhouette in the bottom-right corner with tall thin reeds reaching up against the pale water, rather than adding extra elements like piles or birds.

I'm planning to paint the reeds as hand-defined rigger strokes with tapered pressure, generated in a loop with slight randomization so they read as marks rather than a mechanical pattern. For the horizon, I'll keep the left side open water and sky to preserve the luminous glow, while the right side gets a low headland silhouette with a windmill and a few trees in dark warm-violet.

The earlier attempt made the far shore terrain far too tall and pointy — I need to scale that hill down to a modest low bank (much shorter than before) while keeping the windmill around 45 units tall, since that element previously looked fine. I'll also need to repaint the windmill since it got accidentally covered by the sky layer. For the water, I'm thinking about adding a reflected sun path with glittering horizontal dashes to break up the current flat wash.

Since dry paint won't smear, I can build detail predictably, relying on soft edges or thin glazes for softness where needed. For clouds, I'll paint the body first in mid-tone with soft-edged, flowing filbert strokes, then layer in shadow tones afterward.

For edge softness, I could work within the same wet session—adding shadow and highlight passes while the paint stays open for hours—and use gentle internal blending along the cloud's flow direction to avoid smearing, keeping edits confined within the mask. The `lose()` technique for softening outer fringes worked reasonably on a smaller cloud test, though stippling with thin, tapering coverage might be a more reliable approach for soft edges overall.

A blurred mask like this taps off to zero at the edge and stays full inside, so painting with that as the load function gives thin, tapering veils at the border — soft edge transitions like I've used before with halos. I'm also considering the "glaze" hand for wispy, translucent clouds, since it lays down a thin brushed layer well suited for cirrus-type effects.

Stepping back to the composition, I'm reconsidering whether the current focal cumulus tower is too dominant and hard to render well — maybe a broad stratocumulus bank across the upper right, in perspective with larger bars up high tapering toward the horizon, would read better. I'm imagining mauve-grey shadowed undersides against cream/peach lit edges, with the bars forming diagonal lines that lead the eye.

Now I'm planning out the individual cloud shapes: a few elongated masses positioned around the upper right, mid-right, left, and near-horizon areas, with warmer glowing undersides on the ones closest to the sun and cooler tops elsewhere.

I'm also thinking about adding visible brushstroke texture to the clouds so the sky reads as painted rather than a smooth gradient. Given how much I've already worked through, I want to stay pragmatic and pace myself to wrap things up within the next several chunks, tackling the pink strip fix and clouds first before moving on to the shore, boat, and water details.

Before fixing the pink strip, I realize the cloud reflections in the water depend on the clouds being finished first, so I'll paint those afterward using darker, broken horizontal strokes matching the cloud colors. For now I'll repaint the horizon water on the right with a vertically faded blend so there's no hard edge, matching it to the grey-lilac tones already present nearby.

Then I'll extend down to y=505..530 with the water mix and blend it horizontally against the dried pink strip, letting the wet paint feather smoothly over the opaque layer below.

The horizon gradient looks better now, though I'm noticing a faint vertical seam near x≈720 that likely marks where the image strip boundary used to be.

Some small grey beads still linger along the horizon line at a couple of spots — leftover bits of the old shore silhouette. I'll plan to fold the fix in when I repaint the shore, since that will naturally cover most of them.

Now I'm sketching out the cloud composition, thinking through the sky's color layers and deciding how the clouds should be lit from a low sun near the left horizon, with their undersides catching a warm glow close to the sun's position.

With the sun sitting right at the horizon, light travels horizontally, so I'm reasoning that clouds should be rim-lit on their sun-facing left sides, while their tops stay in cool shadow — mid-altitude clouds especially bright underneath from that low glow, upper clouds more silhouetted. I'm settling on a mid-value mauve-grey cloud mass at top-right, lit along its lower-left edge.

Now I want to add dark stratus bars near the horizon around the sun, silhouetted against the glow with a warm rim underneath, plus wispy high clouds catching pink light at mid-left. For the brushwork I'm planning soft horizontal filbert strokes blended within a feathered mask to fuse the edges, and I'm starting to lay out the outline points for the first big cloud mass, thinking through how its base should slope given the perspective.

I want the lit side to read as left/underside so it doesn't look like a flat cutout. This upper-right mass balances the sun glow at lower left, with the shoreline and mill anchoring the right side and the boat centered below — good asymmetry overall. To avoid a cheap-sunset feel, I need varied edge softness, cauliflower lumps only where light hits, and values kept in a controlled mid-range.

For the actual painting sequence, I'm laying down a soft-edged shadow base along the cloud's top contour first, then building smaller lump shapes at decreasing sizes toward the upper-left, adding light tones on the sun-facing rims, and finishing with a horizontal blend pass within the masked area.

I'm weighing whether to define the lumps as separate soft-edged outline shapes or use a stippling technique for cauliflower-like texture that would fuse nicely on the wet layer underneath. I think it'll work better to iterate and check results as I go rather than over-plan, keeping chunks manageable and tracking drying state, and I'm confirming that the cloud color piles I need were already set up as persistent globals earlier.

Now I'm working out the lighting logic more concretely: with sun low and left, the cloud gets warm light on its left/underside and cool blue-grey shadow on top/right, giving it that contre-jour silver-lining glow along the sun-facing edge while the body stays mauve-grey.

I'm mixing specific paint piles for each zone—body shadow, deeper shadow, and midtone—each built from lead white, smalt, cobalt blue, red earth, and raw umber in varying ratios to capture that warm-cool contrast.

Now I'm rethinking the approach for painting each cloud lump: rather than treating them as ellipsoid forms with mechanical tonal steps, I want to build them like a painter would—laying a dark base tone across the whole shape, then adding a smaller lit shape offset toward the light source with its own soft outline, then blending the two together rather than just offsetting a copy of the coordinates.

Actually, trying smooth form-value loads across piles didn't work well before—the results looked like flat cutouts with hard bright rims, likely because the silhouette mask edge wasn't soft enough. I should instead try painting the cloud with pure freehand brushwork, no masks at all: layered horizontal curved strokes with tapering pressure using a wide flat brush.

A hybrid approach seems best: use masked work for the soft mass falloff, then a few direct strokes for edge accents. I'm setting up a base outline mask with soft character and moderate lobe, then layering a filbert brush pass over it with horizontal angle, varied stroke length, and soft-edged fill sourced from a blurred version of the mask.

Before painting I want to sanity check the geometry by printing the mask area, and clip strokes to the crisp mask boundary while letting the load fade from the blurred mask so bristles thin out naturally at the edges rather than painting hard into the sky. Time to just try it and see how it looks.

Real water isn't a perfect mirror though — Fresnel reflectance varies with angle, so it's brighter near the horizon and lets more of the water's own dark color show through near the viewer, and ripples break up the reflection further. I want to plan the water's color scheme based on the sky above it: near the horizon it should closely mirror the golden-apricot tones, then as it descends it should reflect progressively higher parts of the sky (cream, peach, pale blue), while also naturally darkening and cooling with depth due to the water's own color and rippling, eventually settling into a darker blue-teal at the bottom.

Now I'm sketching out a light-value map for the whole scene, assigning approximate brightness values to the sky, sun core, water bands, light path, and silhouetted elements like the land, boat, and posts, so I can plan a strong glowing light path down the center that pops against darker surrounding water. Then I'm outlining a staged approach to painting the water, starting with a base layer of horizontal strokes on top of the dried underpainting.

For that base water layer, I'm planning shorter, choppier strokes than the sky's smoother streaks, using a flat brush with angle jitter and opaque coverage to get a textured but controlled look. After that base, I'll layer in the golden glare path, then add ripple lines that thin and densify toward the horizon, and finally paint in reflections of the land, clouds, and boat.

Now I'm defining specific color mixtures and value stops for the water at each vertical position, working from warm golden creams near the top down through cooler grays.

Continuing down to the darkest tone at the bottom, then I'm shifting to the right variant beneath the pink cloud, which runs warmer with rose and lilac hues, working out lead white, vermilion, and smalt ratios at each height down through y=590.

I want the color stops to darken strongly toward the bottom, matching the existing water's palette closely so I can just overlay opaque strokes for texture and contrast. I'm sketching out a general strips function that takes region masks, color stops for both sides, and stroke jitter parameters, varying stroke length and angle so the strokes read as ripples rather than uniform streaks.

For the brush calls, I'll keep fill=true on the broad-hand strokes since that coverage style worked well in the sky earlier, even if it risks looking blobby. For W1, I'm planning roughly 17 overlapping strips from y=497 to 745, doubled for both sides, with stroke width narrowing near the horizon and widening at the bottom to fake perspective.

function wstopc(ST, y, med)
  for i = 1, #ST - 1 do
    local a, b = ST[i], ST[i+1]
    if y <= b[1] or i == #ST - 1 then
      local t = clamp((y - a[1]) / (b[1] - a[1]), 0, 1)
      return mixp(a[2], b[2], t, med or 0.05)

  end
end

The water now has richer horizontal brushy bands, which I prefer over the flat slab, but it still needs the light path and glitter, the reflection of the mauve bank and rose cloud, and foreground darks. Taking stock after roughly 223 chunks, I'm reviewing the overall composition: a sky with a nice gradient and a mauve strata bar on the left.

The rose cloud at upper right looks cut out with too-hard edges and mottled texture, the dark shore at right with the windmill reads nicely, and the water shows horizontal strips that are currently too regular and stepped. My next steps are to lightly blend the water with a gentle horizontal pass to soften the banding while keeping some streak texture, then address the cloud's crisp cotton-candy outline by softening its edges.

For the cloud specifically, I need to reconsider the light logic — with the sun low on the horizon to the left, the cloud's left-facing side should catch warm rose/gold light while the tops stay in cool blue-grey shade, which is roughly what's there now but too flat. I need stronger contrast: deeper blue-grey mauve shadows in the crevices between lobes against brighter warm highlights on the sunlit flanks, and I should check whether the paint from four and a half hours ago is still workable or has started to gel.

The smooth ellipsoid lumps I painted are making the cloud look cut-out and cartoonish with their scalloped edges, so rather than clean silhouettes I should break up the outline with irregular, painterly strokes — using a soft edge-drag technique to erode the cloud's boundary and adding sky-coloured wisps along the edge to disrupt the uniform bumps.

I should also work efficiently across the whole piece rather than obsessing over one area: the sky needs some subtle upper structure like wispy cirrus streaks while staying calm overall, and the left strata bar is too flat and mauve — I want to rework it into long horizontal dark bars with warm lit undersides, soft dissolving ends, a lighter pink upper edge, and glow from the sun shining under and partly through.

Since the paint is fully dry now, I can overpaint the odd domed shape at the top of the strata with sky color to erase it, then repaint thinner, more elegant bars — three horizontal slivers of varying length with tapered ends. For the water, I need to add the sun's vertical glitter path and reflections: a soft dark smear below the horizon for the mauve bar, vertical dark streaks for the reflected land on the right, and a pinkish smear for the rose cloud reflection.

I'm picturing a small dark sailing boat crossing the glitter path as a focal point, with its reflection below — maybe a fishing boat with a brown lug sail. For the foreground, I'll add mooring piles with reflections at the bottom corner and dark reeds for depth, plus a few tiny bird silhouettes near the cloud for life. Since the water is still wet, I should blend it lightly now and wait for it to dry before adding the glitter details.

The water gradient looks good with its smooth horizontal strokes, so I'll let it dry before adding the light path, glitter, and reflections. I'm working out the sun's position at the horizon and planning the reflection column beneath it as a straight strip of broken horizontal glitter dashes widening toward the viewer.

Since the sun's hidden behind low strata, I'll soften the path but keep the horizon glow bright cream, tapering into the foreground with layered horizontal dashes that grow in length and thickness with distance -- tiny and dense near the horizon, wider and sparser up front, using warm white tones from lead white and chrome yellow at the top.

Further down I'm mixing in yellow ochre and pale smalt for softer cream tones, with dark blue-grey dashes for the wave troughs sitting beneath. I'm considering whether `stipple` with a horizontal drag length and variable coverage function would give more natural short dashes than manually placing strokes with `work`.

I want to work out the math for stipple coverage on a small round tool—a touch covers roughly 2 square units at width 2, so covering a 40000-unit path region at 0.3 density needs about 6000 touches, taking roughly 33 minutes. That seems fine, so I'll let the water layer dry for about 8 days before continuing, and use that time to finish the strata bar and cloud once they've set.

For the strata bar rework, instead of removing the whole old mauve bar and repainting the sky glow gradient underneath, it's easier to keep the bar as a base and refine it—softening edges and adding lit structure—then hide the problematic dome section with local glow-colored strokes blended into the surrounding yellow.

Actually, a better idea: turn the dome into a cumulus tower rising from the bar, dark mauve with a bright warm rim on the sun-facing side, since it's positioned just left of the sun—that's a classic sunset silhouette look, though I'd want to break up its currently too-symmetrical semicircle top with irregular edges.

I think it's more efficient to accept some roughness here and instead focus on making elements read as coherent through rim lighting and soft edges using `lose`. Let me take a closer look at the left bar to figure out next steps.

That bar looks flat and lifeless, and the dome resembles a bald head, so I want to repaint the whole area as a convincing strata cloud bank lit from behind at sunset—dark mauve-blue-grey silhouette masses up top, with an apricot glow rimming the underside near the horizon.

I'm thinking of layered, staggered strata that dissolve into the glow, plus a cumulus mass rising on the left, rather than overpainting everything from scratch—better to build the new shapes directly over the old bar using its mauve tone as underpainting, reshaping the dome into irregular cumulus lobes and thinning the whole band for more elegance. This bar's real job is to add dark contrast near the sun and create depth in the composition.

Reconsidering the whole scene: the main mass should really be the right cumulus and dark headland, with this left bar acting as a counterweight—so it should stay thin and low, with a glowing lower edge and a few atmospheric horizontal streaks rather than a heavy block. Simplest path is covering the old bars in glow tones (apricot-cream gradient) built from color strips I've already worked out, then drawing thinner bars with soft edges on top, reusing the sun-glow layering I set up earlier in this same region.

Since each new pass uses fresh random seeds, the patch won't replay identically, but that's fine—the blend only fuses wet paint, so it acts as a discrete overlay. To avoid visible seams where the new coat meets the dried glow, I want to feather the patch edges through load falloff, keep the paint thin but opaque, and match colors carefully. I'm also considering an alternative: instead of dark bars, turn them into bright glowing cloud shapes near the sun rather than dark silhouettes.

Thinking about the physical lighting logic, clouds between the viewer and the sun should read as dark silhouettes with bright rims, while clouds farther from the sun are lit warm from below or the side—consistent with my existing plan. So I'll proceed with the patch approach at a moderate scale and then paint the new bars, though I'm also weighing whether to instead just add layers directly onto the existing mauve bar to reshape it.

Since the bar is dry, new paint sits on top, so I'll try reshaping in place: cover the domed top with glow-colored paint, add a thin broken warm rim light along the upper edge, darken and cool the body, blend a warm apricot glow into the underside, and soften the top edges against the glow to break up the flatness of the single value.

Actually I'm considering just overpainting the whole region with the glow recipe since I have reliable functions for it, covering x from -15 to 570 and y from 330 to 497 — and since the surrounding sky glow was built with the same recipe, this patch should blend seamlessly.

But I'm weighing whether it's better to mask just the bars themselves, grown by a margin with soft falloff, rather than a full rectangle — a hard rectangular boundary risks a visible seam if my recolor doesn't perfectly match the surrounding glow, whereas a mask-limited patch would blend more naturally into the existing paint.

Writing patch strip code...

Actually I'm second-guessing whether removing the bars entirely is worth it, versus an in-place approach that preserves more of the original information — trying to weigh which gives the cleaner final result.

I've decided a fresh cover is better since the bars were flawed. Now I'm designing new, thinner bars with more variety: a main long bar drifting toward the horizon near the sun in dark mauve-blue with a warm apricot rim, plus a short upper bar and a small wispy accent above it.

Above that I want a couple of thin cirrus streaks catching orange light, elongated and horizontal, avoiding the earlier flat-mauve mistake by using deeper, varied color with lit rims. I need to make sure the water has dried before painting the sky patch, since it's masked separately from the horizon and lower wet areas so my strokes won't bleed across.

events.text: size 1000

The sky now has a clean, warm glow, but it feels a bit flat and lacks contrast—the large gradient bands still look overly "computed." I'm thinking through what moves would push it toward a stronger finish, weighing the risks against what I've learned about the simulator: dry paint accepts new opaque strokes cleanly with crisp edges, while wet paint blends, drags, and gets muddy when dark tones hit wet light areas.

Taking stock of the composition so far, I have the sky gradient, a peach-rose cloud with a mauve shadow that reads flat and cut-out, the windmill and grove silhouette on the right, a grey-blue water gradient with pink near the horizon, and a yellow glow on the left. Still missing are the dark cloud bars near the sun that need repainting with better technique, the light path on the water, a foreground element like a boat or figure for scale, softened cloud edges and sky texture, water ripples and reflections, and deeper contrast overall with a darker sky top and water bottom. The cloud's hard edge and blotchy patches bother me most, so I want to soften that edge next.

Since the paint has dried, I can now paint over it opaquely and control the edges by blending sky-colored strokes into select spots and adding crisp rim-light highlights. Thinking through what this sunset seascape needs most: the sun glow, its shimmering reflection on the water, dark silhouetted shapes for contrast, and the cloud's rim-light, with a foreground-to-background value progression for depth. I'm leaning toward adding a small dark rowing boat with a silhouetted figure crossing the light path on the water to anchor the composition and draw the eye.

I'm weighing boat placement and scale options against the horizon line, then settling on a small sailing barge with a single lug sail positioned mid-ground where it catches warm light, hull and mast sized modestly with its reflection below, plus maybe a few gull silhouettes in the sky for life — keeping it restrained rather than overloading the scene. Before adding these elements though, I want to fix the overall tonal structure first.

Looking at the water, it's too flat and gray right now with no real reflection of the sunset sky, so I'm working out how to paint a shimmering light path using short, irregular horizontal strokes of pale yellow-white that trace the sun's glow down toward the viewer, figuring out how that column should narrow or widen along its length.

I'm planning the dashes for the sun's reflection widening as it descends toward the viewer, plus a soft pinkish smear for the cloud's reflection and darker wobbly vertical shapes beneath the land and mill.

Thinking back on the cloud bar attempt that came out flat and cut-out looking, I realize the fix is to build it in tonal layers - soft on the upper edge but with a crisp warm rim below, rather than one hard-edged slab.

Since the sky is dry, only the bar's wet paint smears horizontally across it as a thin film, which reads as a soft edge without disturbing the sky — that's consistent with how I used blend with clip disabled before, and it avoids the earlier "ears" issue that came from wet-on-wet contact. Beyond edges though, natural-looking bars really depend on shape: irregular widths, tapered ends, and a few small detached wisps rather than uniform slabs, so I want to draw them with varied control points instead of straight parallel lines.

With plenty of time budget left, I can keep iterating — maybe adding faint cirrus streaks in the upper sky for texture, though the current horizontal striping already reads nicely as brushwork so I don't want to overdo it. I'm also reconsidering the right cumulus cloud, which currently looks like flat pink candy floss; I should give it a darker mauve-grey shadowed underside, pale gold lit tops, and a bright rim light on the sun-facing edge since the sun is low on the left.

Actually, thinking through the light direction more carefully — since the sun sits at the horizon and the cloud is high up, the underside and left faces should glow warm gold-pink while the top faces away into cooler shadow. That's the classic backlit sunset cloud look, so I want to push the contrast further: darker blue-grey tops around value 0.35 against a glowing gold underbelly.

Since that paint layer has dried, I can repaint the cloud fresh with a better lobed outline, blending wet for softer, feathery transitions. I'm also reconsidering its scale — it's roughly 430 by 230 units, quite dominant in the upper right, so I might keep the footprint but refine the shape to feel less pasted-on. The bigger quality gain will come from varied brushwork, edge work, and small focal details, so I'll tackle the boat as the focal point first, then water sparkle, then the cloud bars, then return to refine the large cloud before final glazes.

Thinking through sequencing more carefully: since layers overlap, order matters — water needs to go down first with its light path and reflections, then the boat painted over it once dry, then sky elements. For the water's light path, I'm planning the geometry as a path centered at x=300 that widens gradually going down the canvas, then generating individual short horizontal dash strokes along that path with randomized offsets and lengths to create a natural sparkle effect.

I'm working out the visual logic: dashes should be longer and brighter near the horizon and center, with jitter in position and brush width, using pale yellow-white tones near the horizon fading to warmer, sparser marks toward the foreground. I'm weighing whether a rule-based dash field still counts as genuine brushwork rather than a computed pattern, deciding it fits the spirit since each individual mark remains a deliberate brush stroke.

Next I'm planning the reflections of the darker elements — the land mass reflecting as a broken dark vertical band and the mill's wobbly thin reflection — both painted with thinned strokes over the pinkish water using short horizontal touches for a rippled effect. Then I move on to designing the small sailing boat.

I'm working out placement: sail height around 65-70 units with the hull waterline near y≈556, straddling the horizon line at 497 so the sail silhouettes partly against the glowing sky and partly against water. I'm also considering positioning the boat near x≈330, close to the sun's light path at x=300, for a dramatic silhouette effect against the glitter.

A small dark boat silhouetted against the glowing water band reads as elegant and distant, with a second smaller one further along; but the bottom third stays too empty, so I'm considering adding a foreground element like a mooring post or a partially cropped rowing boat at the corner as a repoussoir device to add scale, depth, and texture to the dark water.

Simpler than a boat, I think 2-3 leaning wooden pilings rising from the bottom with rim light on their sun-facing edges and wobbly reflections would evoke a Dutch harbor well — with the tallest post extending from the bottom edge up past the horizon line for real foreground presence.

I'm now weighing where to place them: too central and they'd block the sun, so I'm considering the lower right instead, around x≈830-900, shorter and tilted with a mooring rope, mostly silhouetted against the dark water with just their edges catching rim light.

Actually, since foreground water near the viewer reflects the darker upper sky while the horizon reflects the bright glow, a dark foreground element won't read well there unless something else lights it—maybe a small boat silhouette would work better for contrast.

On a 500mm canvas that's roughly 20mm tall, small enough for a simple silhouette with a round brush — a circular head, tapered body, thin pole. I could simplify to just a sailboat, but a lone punter figure adds human scale and life, so I'll keep it minimal: dark vertical shape, small hat, thin pole. Now I'm also considering the large expanse of empty water in the lower third of the canvas, roughly a third of the total height.

For the water, once the base layer is dry, I want to build up a glowing light path down the center using flat strokes with soft falloff in pale yellow, then add scattered glitter dashes, some darker reflection accents, and subtle horizontal ripple strokes that get denser and larger toward the bottom to break up the smoothness and give it a sense of luminous depth.

I want to test this on a small region first before committing to the full image, since each stroke is permanent though I could paint over with base water if needed. I'll try a small area, x 200-400, y 560-620, to see how the glitter dashes actually look before scaling up.

function arc_pts(cx, cy, rx, ry, a0, a1, n, wob, seed)
  local pts = {}
  for i = 0, n do
    local a = lerp(a0, a1, i / n)
    local k = 1 + wob * math.sin(i * 1.9 + seed)
    pts[#pts+1] = {cx + rx * k * math.cos(a), cy + ry * k * math.sin(a)}

  return pts

Looking at the whole canvas now, I see the swatch outlines lingering at bottom right, the island's left half smeared over with pale sky wash, and the cloud sitting as a flat salmon lump. I'm mapping out remaining work, starting with repainting the island's silhouette crisply and dark—hill, trees, and windbreak.

Then comes modelling the cloud, adding sparse dry-brush strata near the sun rather than sausage-like streaks, darkening the too-pale foreground water with ripples and the island's reflection while painting out the swatch remnants, adding a dark-hulled boat with a backlit sail on the light path, framing the foreground with posts, reeds and dark vignette corners, and finishing with a bright sun disc and glare at the horizon.

The key compositional move is boosting contrast and giving the piece a focal point: a small silhouetted sailboat around (300, 560), sitting right on the sun's light path, dark against a warm glow since the light comes from behind it.

Now I'm working out how to fix the foreground water itself, which currently reads as flat, low-contrast slabs of pale grey-blue. I want to darken it and add horizontal ripple strokes that catch light like sky reflections, growing larger toward the bottom, though I'm weighing whether short round-brush dashes or wavy ribbon shapes will read better as waves without looking like scribbles.

I'm settling on painting several long horizontal ribbons with a flat brush along a slightly wavy path, loaded with pale sky color fading into the dark wet base—spaced tighter near the horizon and wider at the bottom, since laying wet paint over dry lets these strokes sit crisply on top. Then I'm sketching out the overall value structure for the finished piece: a dark-mid deep blue sky up top, a dark-to-mid cloud mass with warm rims in the upper right, and I'm still working out the middle ground.

I'm mapping out the horizon and foreground next—a bright glowing sky around the sun, a crisp horizon line with a dark island and a few low dark strata bars, and water that's brightest in a central path but darker toward the bottom and sides, framed by dark posts at the foreground edges with the boat sitting dark against the path. To add depth I'm leaning toward mooring posts in the left foreground, tall and dark, possibly with a small cormorant perched on one for a nice focal touch.

Settling on three posts of varying height leaning slightly, with a bird on one, creates a repoussoir effect and clear foreground/midground/background layering. I'm placing a small silhouetted fishing sailboat with a dark lug sail in the mid-distance on the light path, with its reflection streaking below, and considering adding a few gull silhouettes near the sun for extra life in the scene.

I want to soften the horizon slightly with a thin sun-bleached band rather than a perfectly hard edge, keeping it crisp but atmospheric. For the island repaint, I'll redo the hill silhouette with trees, windmill, and tower in dark, crisp opaque strokes, since the previous version got smeared when the sky was repainted over it.

That's probably from my blend at chunk 255 with the mask extending to x=780, plus the sky rows painted in chunk 254 up to x=700. I should zoom in at 1:1 to check the actual current state of the island.

I realize the island looks like a semi-transparent grey scumble where sky strokes piled over the dry paint. I want to repaint the island entirely opaque and dark, so I'm going to design its silhouette carefully once instead of redrawing it repeatedly, working out where the horizon sits.

The headland rises from a thin low strip into a knoll with a windmill, dips, then climbs into a wooded rise with rounded tree crowns and a slender pointed church spire — a small Dutch village. I'm picturing tiny warm-lit roof accents in vermilion and ochre catching the sun against the dark silhouette, with the base color mixed from bone black, raw umber, and Prussian blue for a deep blue-brown.

For the distant island itself, though, aerial perspective means it should read dark violet-grey rather than black, so I'm mixing raw umber, smalt, bone black, red earth, and lead white for a softer dark tone, plus a lighter haze band near the waterline where the atmosphere glows. I'll define the island's edge with a firm, fine outline, then add its reflection below the horizon as dry-brush horizontal streaks in dark violet, painted with a low-load flat brush for texture.

Before repainting the silhouette solidly, I need to make sure the new dark mask fully covers all the old paint layers underneath — the shore, land mask, grove, trees, and mill parts — using high opacity and a mask that's a superset of all those old shapes, otherwise grey remnants of the previous painting will peek out around the edges.

I recall this same patch-and-dry approach worked well for the sky in that zone earlier.

Alternatively, I could just cover the entire union of all the old island mask variants with one big dark opaque shape, since those masks were similar enough in size that the union wouldn't distort the island silhouette much, while guaranteeing every grey remnant gets buried underneath.

Reality confirms this: sunset clouds glow warm on their undersides from light bouncing up from below the horizon, with the tops staying in cool blue-grey-mauve shadow. function cst(T, med)
